{"grade": 6, "complete": false, "main_gap": "Lemma 1's proof invokes a false 'infinite sunflower fact' for families of unbounded set size; only the bounded-size version actually used is valid, and the restriction is never made explicit.", "errors": [{"description": "The quoted sunflower fact is false without a size bound (e.g. the nested chain {1},{1,2},{1,2,3},... has no infinite subfamily with constant pairwise intersection), and the sketched induction (delete a repeated element and 'continue') only terminates for bounded-size families. Hence Lemma 1 as stated is unproven; only the 'In particular' bounded-size claim (all that is later used, via |D| ≤ a_1) is justified, after a one-line pigeonhole to a fixed cardinality.", "quote": "every infinite family of distinct finite sets has an infinite subfamily $X_{i_1},X_{i_2},\ldots$ for which there is a fixed set $R$ satisfying"}, {"description": "Statement (2) needs upward-closedness of F (if S contains C in C then S in F). This follows immediately from (1) but is never stated; the text only justifies the direction 'every member of F contains a member of C'.", "quote": "Thus $\mathcal C$ is an intersecting antichain, and
\[
S\in\mathcal F
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\text{ contains some }C\in\mathcal C.
\]"}], "notes": "The core argument (support-determined acceptance, self-duality, weight descent via the rejected squarefree witness w(S)≥a_1, bounded terminal supports, periodicity mod L) is correct, well-organized and yields the full conclusion for all n. Deduction only for the overstated sunflower lemma."}
